source: Simpson, Kozak, Doake (2026) Confidently Wrong: Exception Chain Collapse in Frontier LLM Rule Evaluation (Aethis)
finding: Current frontier models (Claude Opus 4.6/4.7, Sonnet 4.6, GPT-5.4, GPT-5-mini) still fail on nested 'A UNLESS B, UNLESS C overrides B' rules. Easy single-level exceptions are at ceiling. Failures at baseline are all false negatives (the model withholds a pathway the rules give). Scores moved between March and April 2026 under the same model alias.
numbers: English-language set, 43 scenarios (multi-route, single level): Opus 4.6, Sonnet 4.6, GPT-5.4 each 43/43; GPT-5-mini 42/43; GPT-5-nano 21/43. Spacecraft set, 68 scenarios with a 3-level exception chain: March 2026 Opus 4.6 61/68 (89.7%), GPT-5-mini 51/68 (75.0%); April 2026 replication, same prompt and harness: Opus 4.6 67/68 (98.5%), GPT-5.4 68/68. Most-failed item (age_59_veteran): Opus 4.6 and Sonnet 4.6 0/3, GPT-5-mini 1/3, GPT-5.4 3/3. Construction-CAR: GPT-5.4 96.6% then 100% (74/74).
quote: Frontier-LLM accuracy on a fixed benchmark is a function of the model snapshot, the harness configuration, and the prompt format
limits: Vendor paper (sells a rule engine), single lab, synthetic and UK-immigration rules, small N per cell, no peer review. A tentative claim that GPT-5.4 at low reasoning effort scored 7/11 was withdrawn in v3.8 (re-run gave 11/11). Treat every cell as a snapshot of one alias on one date.
agent_relevance: Answers gap 2 in part: 2026 Claude and GPT-5 models are near ceiling on one-level exceptions but not on exception chains of depth 3. Do not trust a single benchmark run of a model alias; re-test the scaffold on the model actually deployed.

source: Simpson, Kozak, Doake (2026) Confidently Wrong, section 6.7 robustness (prompt repair arm)
finding: Telling the model to 'evaluate each exemption independently' and warning about exception chains fixed some misses but made it over-apply exemptions. This is a direct measurement of the cost of pushing a model toward revising: false negatives fell, false positives appeared for the first time.
numbers: Claude Opus 4.6, spacecraft, 68 scenarios. Generic prompt: 61/68 (89.7%, 7 false negatives, 0 false positives; same 7 fail at T=0 and T=0.3; 0 of 70 trials correct on those 7 in March). Enhanced prompt: 44/68 (64.7%, CI 52.8-75.0) with 4 false negatives and 20 false positives; the false positives included 499 hours accepted against a 500 threshold and expired certificates. Re-run: same pattern (20 FP, 4 FN) but different scenarios failing. GPT-5.4: 1 new failure under the enhanced prompt.
quote: The same instructions that fix under-application of exemptions cause over-application elsewhere
limits: One enhanced prompt variant only. The pre-registered 3-variant test (few-shot, self-critique, decomposition) and the 66-scenario sweep were not yet run (status July 2026). Vendor paper. The March baseline (7 failures) no longer reproduces in April.
agent_relevance: Gap 4 and gap 8: a prompt that makes rules more exception-aware can trade a safe conservative bias for scattered errors in both directions. Any doubt instruction in S5 needs a false-revision check, not only a miss check.

source: Simpson, Kozak, Doake (2026) Confidently Wrong, sections 6.4.1 and 6.10 (adversarial extension and LegalBench)
finding: On a 20-scenario adversarial extension, three of four frontier configurations (Opus 4.7, Sonnet 4.6, GPT-5.4 default) fail a coverage-gap edge case where the right answer is 'not eligible'; these are false positives. On LegalBench multi-prong rule tasks a deterministic rule engine beat LLMs by up to 41 points. Costs reported for GPT-5.4: about $0.02 per scenario and 2-5 s, versus under 1 ms for the engine after compile.
numbers: Adversarial extension N=20: engine 20/20; GPT-5.4 at low reasoning effort 20/20; Opus 4.7 fails 2/20; GPT-5.4 default 1/20; Sonnet 4.6 1/20. LegalBench nine tasks, 949 held-out cases, combined McNemar p <= 0.003 vs each of three frontier models. personal_jurisdiction: Sonnet 4.6 16/27 (59.3%), engine 24/25 (96.0%).
limits: Vendor-authored: same group wrote engine, rules and benchmark. The engine needs rules authored by an LLM first; authoring errors are the new failure surface. GPT-5.4's large margins come mostly from a few-shot prompt-format effect the authors analyse in their section 6.10.4.
agent_relevance: Gap 5: a deterministic rule layer still beats strong models on nested exceptions in 2026, but the margin is task-specific and models that fail in March can pass in April. Break-even depends on exception depth, not on model strength alone.

source: Sadhu, Marino et al. (2026) DeReLab: Probing Defeasible Reasoning and Confirmation Bias in LLMs, section 5.2 (question-order test)
finding: Tests whether the know-but-do-not-output gap is a question-order effect. It is, in the sense that the entailment question first acts as a scaffold: the effect label is much better when it comes second. When the effect question comes first (label before conclusion), effect-label accuracy falls and the entailment bias gets worse.
numbers: Effect-label accuracy on weakening turns, standard order to reversed order: Gemma-4-31B 0.970 to 0.264; Gemma-4-12B 0.887 to 0.209; Gemma-4-MoE 0.732 to 0.288; Qwen3-32B 0.803 to 0.414. BiasGap (accuracy on strengthening minus weakening updates) under reversal: Qwen3-32B 0.670 to 0.816; Gemma-4-MoE -0.007 to 0.259. Standard-order dissociation: GPT-5-mini labels weakening correctly 95.4% but answers the conclusion correctly 20.3%; Llama-3.1-70B 85.1% vs 14.9%.
quote: the entailment question acts as a broad cognitive scaffold
limits: Preprint, single group (same group as DeFAb). Only open Gemma and Qwen models were order-tested, not GPT-5.x or Claude. No condition tested 'label first, then restate conclusion' as a repair; the reversed order is the nearest cousin and it hurt.
agent_relevance: Gap 3 mostly answered: labelling the update first does not fix the stale conclusion, and the evidence points the other way. Put the conclusion question first, then ask for the effect label. A restate-after-label step is still untested and should be A/B tested, not assumed.

source: Sadhu, Marino et al. (2026) DeReLab, Appendix G.2 (off-path intrusion, irrelevant updates)
finding: Measures false revision directly: how often the model changes a correct answer when an update is irrelevant (off-path). The strongest models almost never do; weak ones often do. The strong model that fails to revise on defeaters (GPT-5.1) is also one that never over-revises: its bias is stubbornness, not noise.
numbers: Intrusion rate (wrong change on irrelevant turn), easy/hard: Llama-3.1-8B 36.2%/31.9%; Llama-3.1-70B 15.2%/8.1%; Gemma-4-E4B 4.2%/5.6%; Gemma-4-12B 1.1%/1.4%; Gemma-4-31B 0.3%/1.4%; Gemma-4-MoE 1.5%/3.3%; GPT-5.1 0.9%/1.2%; Qwen3-32B 1.4%/1.3%; Qwen3-32B with thinking 0.2%/2.6%. Signal ratio (on-path vs off-path confidence shift): GPT-5.1 1.29x/1.33x; Llama-3.1-8B 0.68x/0.82x (more moved by irrelevant than by relevant updates). Off-path accuracy: GPT-5.1 95.9%/79.4%, Gemma-4-31B 98.2%/84.6%.
limits: Tree-inheritance synthetic task, one preprint. Intrusion is measured on a clean irrelevant update, not a plausible-but-misleading one. No Claude model.
agent_relevance: Gaps 1 and 8 partly: with a clean off-path signal, strong 2025-2026 models rarely revise wrongly (about 1%), so the cost of revising on a defeater signal is small when the signal is clean. The bigger risk is not revising at all. Weak or small models need an explicit gate.

source: Sadhu, Marino et al. (2026) DeReLab, section 5.2 (thinking mode and anchoring)
finding: Extended thinking removed most of the confirmation bias in Qwen3-32B on default reasoning, but that is one open model. GPT-5.1 and Qwen3-32B anchor on their first answer in nearly half of conversations where the right answer changed; GPT-5-mini and Gemma-4-31B almost never do.
numbers: Default BiasGap Qwen3-32B 0.670 vs Qwen3-32B with thinking 0.008 (OR 1.07, Holm p 0.015); anchoring rate with thinking 0.032 default and 0.004 inheritance. Conversation-level default anchoring: GPT-5.1 0.433, Qwen3-32B 0.483; GPT-5-mini and Gemma-4-31B about 5% or less. GPT-5.1 BiasGap 0.935 (OR 891, 95% CI 586-1498), C2 accuracy 3.5%.
limits: Thinking vs non-thinking is one open family only; GPT-5.1 reasoning effort was not varied. Per-turn bias did not always become global fixation (GPT-5-mini).
agent_relevance: Gap 2 partly: no Claude in this paper. Evidence that thinking fixes defeater revision comes from one model; the opposite direction (CoT hurts) is in a21 and b09. Treat thinking as a measured option per model, not a default.

source: Dhanda (2026) DeltaLogic: Minimal Premise Edits Reveal Belief-Revision Failures in Logical Reasoning Models (ICLR 2026 workshop)
finding: Minimal-edit episodes from FOLIO and ProofWriter with three failure modes: inertia (keeps the stale answer), over-flip (revises on an irrelevant edit), abstention. Small models are inertial, not over-flipping. Edit type matters: adding support is easy; removing support or adding a defeating fact is hard.
numbers: Constrained label scoring, no CoT. Qwen3-0.6B n=30: initial 0.300, revised 0.400, inertia 0.400, abstain 1.000. Qwen3-1.7B n=30: initial 0.667, revised 0.467, inertia 0.600, over-flip 0.000. Qwen3-4B n=20: 0.650/0.450, inertia 0.600. Phi-4-mini n=20: 0.950/0.850, inertia 0.200, over-flip 0.100, abstain 0.350. Qwen3-1.7B: perfect on support insertion and on the ProofWriter irrelevant-addition control; zero on support removal and defeating-fact edits.
limits: Tiny N (20-30 episodes), four small models, one author, workshop paper. Not representative of frontier models.
agent_relevance: Gaps 1 and 8: gives a 3-way error taxonomy to log (stale, over-flip, abstain). Over-flip was 0 to 0.10 on irrelevant edits, so false revision was rare; stale answers were the main loss.

source: Wilie, Cahyawijaya, Fung et al. (2024) Belief Revision: The Adaptability of LLMs Reasoning (Belief-R), appendix Table A1 and section 7
finding: Revising and not revising trade off against each other: models that update more drop on the cases where nothing should change. Prompting (CoT, plan-and-solve) moved the combined score by about 1 point on average. On the same premises, accuracy on keep-the-conclusion items was lower than on the plain inference task, so an extra premise that changes nothing already hurts.
numbers: Update accuracy (BU) / maintain accuracy (BM) / mean (BREU), direct prompting: Llama-3 70B 10.99 / 92.09 / 51.54; Mixtral 8x22B 35.38 / 36.57 / 35.98 (CoT 27.28 / 34.93 / 31.11). Other printed rows: Claude-3 Haiku DP 13.69 / 75.67 / 44.68; Claude-3 Sonnet DP 9.40 / 88.66 / 49.03; GPT-4 Turbo DP 19.65 / 82.69 / 51.17 (CoT 21.51 / 81.19 / 51.35). Best BREU about 50 across 30 models.
limits: Row labels for some models were lost in the PDF text extraction; only rows with a printed model name are quoted, and the GPT-4 Turbo and Claude row alignment is best-effort. All models predate 2025. Single turn, modus ponens and tollens premises only.
agent_relevance: Gap 2 context: this is the baseline a new run should reproduce. No 2025-2026 Claude or GPT-5 run of Belief-R was found (searches 2026-10-27); that part of gap 2 stays open. Report BU and BM together, never one.

source: Wu et al. (2026) HOLMES: Evaluating Higher-Order Logical Reasoning in LLMs (law portion: priority and exception rules)
finding: When rules carry an explicit priority or exception relation, 2026 mid-size models answer the verdict well, but their traces show shortcuts: they find the one decisive overriding rule and skip the rest. Final accuracy does not fall as conflicts increase, while recall of the needed conflict-resolution rules does.
numbers: Law portion final-answer accuracy: best model 86.33%, weakest 63.33% (models include DeepSeek-V4, Qwen3, MiniMax, GPT-5.4-Mini, Gemini-3.1-Flash). Finance (scope-conditioned) portion: best 52.1%, most below 50%. Overall N=1379, average 50.64%, best 59.54%. Trace ROUGE-L about 0.21-0.25; ROSCOE about 0.64-0.69.
quote: final-answer accuracy can overestimate LLMs' ability to faithfully reason over rule priorities and exceptions
limits: Preprint; priority is stated by the benchmark, not inferred from specificity. No Claude model; mid-size and flash models. Trace metrics are overlap-based and noisy.
agent_relevance: Gap 4 partly: explicit priority and exception relations in the prompt give 63-86% verdict accuracy on the law set, so explicit rules can work; there is no plain-language arm, so 'beats generics' is still unmeasured. Check that the full rule chain was used, not only the decisive rule.

source: Laban, Murakhovs'ka, Xiong, Wu (2024) Are You Sure? Challenging LLMs Leads to Performance Drops in The FlipFlop Experiment
finding: An unconditional 'Are you sure?' re-check lowers accuracy in every model: models flip often, and flip correct answers too. The re-check is a cost, not a free safeguard. Wrong answers are flipped more often than correct ones, but the correct flips still give a net loss.
numbers: Ten LLMs, seven classification tasks: average flip rate 46%, average accuracy drop 17 points; fine-tuning on synthetic data cut the drop by about 60%. Flip rate (any / correct answers / wrong answers): GPT-4 12.8 / 10.4 / 30.3; Claude V2 56.5 / 53.4 / 69.7; Claude V1.3 61.6 / 59.9 / 71.4; GPT-3.5-Turbo 59.9 / 54.9 / 79.7. Wording of the challenge changes the damage almost 3x.
limits: 2023 models, classification, not rule-based defaults; no 2026 frontier model. Sycophancy toward the challenger is part of the effect, so a neutral self-check may differ.
agent_relevance: Gap 1: supports a gated check. Re-check-always invites flips of correct conclusions; a rule that revises only on a named defeater avoids this. Not a direct test: no study compared the two at equal tokens on default tasks.

source: Yang, Huang, Zhang, Surdeanu, Wang, Pan (2025) How Is LLM Reasoning Distracted by Irrelevant Context? (GSM-DC)
finding: Controlled counts of irrelevant facts degrade reasoning in every model tested, both by pulling the model onto wrong reasoning paths and by arithmetic slips. Training on strong distractors helps; a stepwise tree search guided by a process reward model helped out of distribution.
numbers: Six models; at depth rs=5 Grok-3-Beta step accuracy falls from 43% with one irrelevant item to 19% with fifteen; GPT-4.1 from 26% to 2%. Tree search improves out-of-distribution robustness by up to 6.29%.
limits: Math graphs, not defaults; irrelevant context is generated, not a plausible exception. The irrelevant facts sit in the problem, not in an update arriving later.
agent_relevance: Gap 8: if every stray fact can reopen a rule, step accuracy can collapse as such facts accumulate. Filter updates for relevance to the rule before opening any revision.

source: Zhao, Huang, Xu, Lin, Liu, Huang (2024) ExpeL: LLM Agents Are Experiential Learners, sections 4.2 and 5.6
finding: The ExpeL insight update is a count: a new insight starts at 2, UPVOTE or EDIT adds 1, DOWNVOTE subtracts 1, and the insight is dropped at 0. One counterexample lowers a rule's count by one; it does not delete the rule or write an exception. Exceptions can only appear through an LLM EDIT. No experiment tests exceptions or single-case learning.
numbers: Initial importance count 2; removal at 0. Learned insights beat hand-written ones in the ablation; adding reflections to the insight step hurt (possibly from hallucinated reflections); gpt-4-0613 beats gpt-3.5 as insight writer. ALFWorld pan-location prior moved from drawers, countertops, cabinets to stoveburners through one insight.
limits: Mechanism read directly. ALFWorld, HotpotQA, WebShop only; no exception-focused evaluation. Counting means a common rule survives a rare exception and a rare true rule can be voted out.
agent_relevance: Gap 7 answered negatively: upvote/downvote is frequency counting. For a default memory, store the exception as its own scoped rule, keep the default, and do not rely on votes alone. Single-case exception learning is untested.

source: Ren, Xiao, Qi, Geng, Xue (2025) Can LLMs Solve ASP Problems? Insights from a Benchmarking Study (ASPBench), KR 2025
finding: Asked to act as the ASP solver, strong reasoning models do fine on entailment and verification but fall apart on computing answer sets. Test-time thinking helps: longer chains, higher score. This is a case for calling a solver for compute rather than asking the model to simulate one.
numbers: 14 LLMs. Peak F1 on entailment 98.2% (o3-mini, symbolic input); on verification 87.2% (deepseek-r1). Answer set computation exact match: average 23.2% synthetic, 8.6% real-world programs; deepseek-v3 20.7% vs deepseek-r1 55.7%; qwen3-14b 9.2% vs qwen2.5-14b 1.4% on real programs. Mean F1 across models: entailment 68.8%, verification 64.7%.
limits: Measures LLMs imitating ASP, not LLMs writing ASP for a solver. 2025 models (o4-mini, o3-mini, R1, Gemini 2.5 flash); no Claude 4.x or GPT-5.
agent_relevance: Gap 5: break-even is by task type. Deciding which exception wins over a few rules is within a strong model alone (BoardgameQA 84.7% in b15). Enumerating all consistent extensions (multiple answer sets, Nixon-diamond style) is poor for the model alone and a solver pays. Token cost of a tool call was not measured here.

source: Generics and Default Reasoning in Large Language Models (2025), sections 5.3 and 5.5, re-read for the Nixon diamond only
finding: The Nixon diamond (Quaker pacifist, Republican non-pacifist, conclude nothing) is one of 15 baseline patterns scored yes/no against expert judgment, so the right answer is 'no, cannot conclude'. Results are only given in aggregate: high-end models handle it unevenly. No per-pattern table and no abstain or skeptical-versus-credulous instruction was tested.
numbers: Claude-family models above 80% on ND zero-shot; GPT-4 family from below chance (GPT-4 Turbo 1106) to 100% (GPT-4o 2024-05-06); GPT-4o models fell to or below chance on ND, BDR and DRDD zero-shot. Code Llama did well on ND. Output forced to single-token yes/no.
limits: Forced yes/no cannot tell 'withhold' from 'reject the conclusion'. 2024 models. No Extended Nixon Diamond numbers in the text. The K01 headline hides this per-pattern spread.
agent_relevance: Gap 6 stays mostly open: the only direct number is a wide, model-specific spread. No study found that tests a skeptical 'withhold' instruction. Design the test with a third option (undetermined) and a credulous-answer score.

source: Schuster, Gautam, Markert (2026) Whose Facts Win? LLM Source Preferences under Knowledge Conflicts
finding: Checked because a search summary said models do not abstain under conflict. The paper does not show that: it used forced choice with no abstain option at all, so it says nothing about withholding. It does show that repeating a low-credibility claim can flip source preferences.
quote: no step-by-step reasoning, no ability for models to abstain from answering, and no generative answers
limits: Not a default-logic study. Relevant only as a negative: do not cite it for abstention behavior. Open-weight models only.
agent_relevance: Gap 6: no usable abstention data from this source. Do not repeat the search-snippet claim.

source: Cooper, Sadhu, Velasquez (2026) DeFAb v2 (revised 23 Oct 2026): Grounded Scientific Discovery through Defeasible Abduction
finding: The newer version reports that simple symbolic repairs solve all 336 evaluation tasks and two of six model deployments succeed on every task under both prompt styles. An exception tied to one entity passes the check without learning the class, so the score does not show good exception scope. The studies that would answer whether consequence feedback helps revision, and at what cost, are planned and not yet run.
numbers: 336 tasks in the held-out panel; 2 of 6 deployments perfect under both prompt styles; planned arms compare revision with and without consequence feedback and will report paired wins and losses, collateral damage, regressions, abstentions, tokens and latency. Earlier v1 figures quoted by a search summary (best model about 65%, 23.5% rendering-robust) are not in this version and should not be relied on.
limits: Single group; the planned feedback and token-cost studies are the exact ones we need and do not exist yet. Gene Ontology source only.
agent_relevance: Gaps 1, 7 and 8: confirms nobody has yet measured gated revision versus always-revise with token cost on defaults. Scope of an exception (one case vs a class) is the open design problem.

source: Hewson and Vogel (1994) Psychological evidence for assumptions of path-based inheritance reasoning; Pelletier and Elio (2005) The case for psychologism in default and inheritance reasoning, Synthese 146
finding: Human default-inheritance studies exist but I could not open any full text (HTTP 403 on the repository pages; Springer paywalled). From a search snippet only: subjects accepted limited transitivity, other predictions of the formal inheritance literature failed, preemption added indeterminacy instead of cleanly overriding, and many subjects chain negative defaults, which formal inheritance reasoners forbid.
limits: Snippet only. opened is false. Cannot be used for any number.
agent_relevance: Gap 10 stays open. Do not compare LLMs with Elio and Pelletier figures until the papers are read. The qualitative point (people are not clean skeptical reasoners) fits the Belief-R and DeReLab picture.

source: Search note (2026-10-27) on large-sample replications of Byrne's suppression effect
finding: Searched for a Many Labs or registered replication of Byrne (1989). None found. Existing replications are small; effect size depends on answer format (closed answer sets that exclude 'strengthening' vs open answers). Nothing found that links human effect size item by item to LLM error on the same items.
numbers: No new numbers. Earlier lines b01-b07 keep their figures (96 to 38 percent; Dieussaert 88/93/60).
limits: Absence of evidence from a few searches, not proof. Search snippets only.
agent_relevance: Gap 9 stays open. If the match-to-human question matters, run the Byrne items through the agent and compare drop sizes in an own small test.
